newsitem.title: JAPAN: Corporate bad debts, scandals spark JGB rally.
newsitem.headline: Corporate bad debts, scandals spark JGB rally.

text.p: The recent rally in Japanese government bonds (JGB) is backed by "flight to quality" purchases by investors worried over corporate liquidity after a spate of scandals and lingering debt, fund managers say.

"We've sold off some of our corporate bond holdings and switched to JGBs," a senior fund manager at a life insurance firm said. "We are trying to allocate our funds into bonds with higher liquidity and good credit qualities."
The yield of the benchmark 182nd JGB issue hit a record low of 2.250 percent in early afternoon trade on Thursday.
Investors say they are more conscious of liquidity after illegal deal scandals hit some top Japanese corporations.
Ajinomoto Co Inc, a major manufacturer of foodstuffs and seasonings, said on Tuesday that two of its executives had been arrested on suspicion of paying off corporate racketeers with company funds.

Last week, Nomura Securities Co Ltd, Japan's largest broker, said two of its executives made apparently illegal deals and funnelled funds to a corporate client which was linked by Japanese media to a former racketeer.
"Some investors seem to be feeling less comfortable about buying corporate bonds with credit ratings of A minus or below. They are becoming more selective," said a brokerage trader.

With domestic interest rates at record low levels and a further decline unlikely, investors need to pull funds out as quickly as possible when rates actually start rising, the life insurance manager said.
Life insurers have also taken profits from corporate bonds ahead of the fiscal year-end on March 31, fund managers said.
"The insurers are feeling uneasy about reinvesting in corporate bonds after profit-taking, so they are buying JGBs instead," another fund manager at a major insurance firm said.
Traders said bonds issued by construction firms were especially unpopular due to the industry's bad debt problems, and the lack of interest has kept some from trading at all.
There are lingering worries over the financial health of Japan's general contractors because of the hefty amount of debts they have guaranteed, many of them believed to be bad.

Late on Wednesday, construction firm Fujita Corp's 5.3 percent straight bond due October 1998, rated triple B plus by a local credit rating agency, was being offered at a yield of around 6.15 percent. Quotes were unavailable on Thursday.
"At the time of issuance, these (construction) bonds were considered to be good. But we cannot sell them now even if we want to," the first fund manager said.
Investors will likely continue to shun corporate bonds with low credit ratings ahead of the introduction of the "prompt corrective action" (PCA) system in April 1998, traders said.

The proposed system will use capital adequacy ratios as a major gauge of the soundness of financial institutions, and will classify corporate bonds with ratings of BBB or above under the same asset category as JGBs, municipal bonds and government-guaranteed bonds.
If the issuer's financial condition is judged as questionable, its corporate bonds will be placed in lower categories, according to Ministry of Finance guidelines.
